opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think there's a single clean metric, and I'm wary of anyone who claims to have one. The way I think about it is to ask, for each of the main ways things could go badly as AI systems become extremely capable, whether we're building the tools to notice the problem and the ability to act on it before it's too late.

So I break it into a few questions. First, can we tell what we're dealing with? Are our evaluations good enough that if a model had dangerous capabilities, like meaningfully helping someone build a bioweapon or undermining human oversight, we'd actually catch it, rather than finding out after deployment? Second, if we found a problem, do we have mitigations that work under real adversarial pressure? That means security strong enough to keep model weights from being stolen, safeguards that hold up against determined misuse, and alignment techniques that don't just make a model look well-behaved on our tests. Third, are we making real progress on the deeper scientific problems, like interpretability and understanding whether a model's stated reasoning reflects what's actually driving its behavior? Those are the things you'd really want before you trust systems that might be smarter than the people overseeing them.

When I put it that way, my honest answer is that some pieces look better than I would have guessed a few years ago and some look worse. On the positive side, there's real institutional machinery now: commitments about what you have to demonstrate before scaling further, dedicated teams doing threat modeling, and interpretability work that has gone from basically nothing to producing results that change how people think about these systems. That's not nothing.

But I don't want to oversell it. The honest picture is that capabilities are moving fast, and a lot of the safety work is still more "we'd probably notice some of the problems" than "we have a reliable solution." Security against highly resourced attackers is genuinely hard. Alignment of systems much more capable than us is still, to a large degree, an open research problem. And no single company gets to decide how this goes. A lot of the risk lives in the overall ecosystem: what other developers do, what governments do, and whether there are norms and rules that keep the cautious actors from being outcompeted.

So my bottom line is something like this. I judge progress less by asking "is it solved?" and more by asking "are we on a trajectory where, if things get scary, we'll know and we'll be able to slow down or adapt?" On that question I'd say we're partway there, there's a lot of work left, and the margin for complacency is pretty thin. I think it's worth being clear-eyed about both halves of that.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't have a confident "on track" verdict, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who did. The problem is that we don't actually know what the challenges of AGI are going to look like in detail. We have a bunch of guesses, and the whole point of the safety work is to be prepared for a range of scenarios, some of which we're probably not even imagining right now.

So instead of asking "are we on track," I tend to break it into a few questions I can actually get some traction on.

The first is: are we doing the things that would be embarrassing not to have done if things go badly? That's stuff like having a serious responsible scaling policy that actually binds behavior, running evaluations for dangerous capabilities before deploying models, investing in interpretability so we're not totally flying blind about what's happening inside these systems, and having the security to not just hand the model weights to anyone who wants them. On that front, I think Anthropic is doing a lot of the right things. I'd also say I'm not an unbiased observer here, so people should discount accordingly.

The second question is: when we find problems, do we actually learn things and change course? And I think this is where I'd push back a little on the framing of "on track." Honestly, a lot of what we've learned over the last couple of years has been about how models behave in ways we didn't predict, and the response to that matters more to me than whether the original plan survived. A safety program that never gets surprised is probably a safety program that isn't looking hard enough.

The third question, and this is the uncomfortable one, is: is the pace of safety progress keeping up with the pace of capability progress? And here I'd say no, not obviously. Capabilities have been moving extremely fast. Interpretability is making real progress, but it's not at the point where you could look at a frontier model and confidently say "this thing isn't going to do something catastrophic in a situation we haven't tested." Alignment techniques work pretty well on the models we have, but we don't have strong guarantees they'll keep working as models get more capable and potentially more strategic. So if you asked me "could Anthropic today safely deploy a system that's much smarter than its own researchers," I'd say I don't think anyone can honestly answer yes to that.

What I'd add is that Anthropic's bet was never that one company could solve this alone. The theory is more like: if powerful AI is coming regardless, it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier, demonstrating that you can take safety seriously and still be competitive, and pushing for industry norms and government policy that raise the floor for everyone. So part of how I judge it is whether that broader ecosystem is moving. And there I'd say there's been meaningful progress, with things like the safety commitments across labs and government AI safety institutes, but it's fragile and it's a lot slower than I'd want.

So my overall take is something like: the right things are being attempted, the organization is pretty serious about it, and we're still not where we need to be. Those three things are all true at once, and I think it would be a mistake to collapse them into a single thumbs up or thumbs down.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between making progress on safety and having a convincing case that you can handle the risks of AGI. Those are pretty different bars. You can be doing useful research, hiring good people, and improving your models’ behavior, without yet having evidence that your approach will work when the systems are much more capable.

What I’d want to look at is: What are the dangerous capabilities you’re anticipating? How would you detect them before deployment? What safeguards would you need at that point, and what evidence would show that those safeguards actually work? And if you reach that point before you have the safeguards, what happens? Are you prepared to pause?

That last question matters a lot. A safety plan should constrain what you do in circumstances where following it is costly. Otherwise, it’s hard to distinguish it from an aspiration.

So I wouldn’t give a confident, blanket answer that Anthropic is on track. I’d want to assess particular commitments and particular results, and I’d want those assessments to be open to serious outside scrutiny. The central question is whether the evidence for safety is keeping pace with the capabilities—not just whether the safety work is getting better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it’s very hard to tell. There’s a difference between making progress on safety research and having good reason to believe you can safely build and deploy a much more capable system. You can be doing valuable work on the first without having established the second.

The question I’d want to ask is: what are the things a future model could do that would make it dangerous, what evidence would convince us those risks are adequately controlled, and what happens if we don’t have that evidence? Does development slow down? Does deployment stop? Who makes that call?

I’d look at Anthropic’s research, but I’d also look at how its commitments translate into decisions as capabilities increase. Are the evaluations strong enough to catch the problems we’re worried about? Are there people actively trying to find ways the safeguards fail? And is there enough outside scrutiny that we aren’t just relying on the company’s own judgment?

So I wouldn’t give a confident verdict that they’re on track. I’d want to see an increasingly concrete safety case, with the willingness to stop if that case can’t be made.
